Stop Overpaying for Uber: How to Score Senior Discounts on Rideshare Apps
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 7:36 AM CDT 5 min read
A little more than a decade ago, getting into a stranger's car and telling them where to take you would be viewed as ill-advised at best. But with the rise of rideshare apps like Uber, Lyft and others, nothing seems more ordinary. The system comes with a lot of benefits; it tends to be cheaper than traditional taxis, it works effectively in most places and you can get practically wherever you want to go.
Combine the rideshare phenomenon with more traditional modes of transportation, and the world has gotten more mobile than ever before with plenty of options to travel. Alas, almost all those options still cost money. Luckily for seniors, there are also plenty of opportunities to save money while getting around.
Want more ways to save money? Sign up for The Penny Hoarder's free newsletter today.
How to Score Senior Discounts on Ridesharing Apps
The bigger rideshare companies all have their own apps, and if you know what to look for, there are loads of ways to save.
When using any of these apps, keep an eye out for promo codes that can help you save even more. In recent promotions, Lyft and Uber both advertise promo codes which give up to 50% discounts to new riders, regardless of your age.
Lyft doesn't offer a generalized senior discount for their basic service, but through their Lyft Silver program, seniors can use a simplified interface, find better vehicle matches (easier entry and exit) and get support to book their ride through Lyft.
Lyft's subscription service Lyft Pink does offer discounts with plans starting at $9.99 (or $99/year). For those who need to travel on a regular basis or have a busy schedule, Pink can help you save a bundle.
Additionally, many cities partner with Lyft to offer discounted rides to those 60 and older. In Charleston, South Carolina, CARTA offers seniors Lyft or Uber trips for as little as $5 each way within a fixed-route area.
Similar to Lyft, Uber doesn't offer a specific senior discount, but it does partner with municipalities to offer discounted rides for those 60 and older.
Also similar to Lyft, if you're a frequent rider, you can save money with a membership. An Uber One membership costs $9.99 (or $96/year) and lets you earn 5% back on rides and includes a $0 delivery fee for food and grocery orders.
GoGoGrandparent.com connects you to rideshare services and arranges deliveries of groceries and medications. Despite the name, anyone over 18 can order a ride and you can use it from any phone that generates tones by the press of a button — meaning, you don't need a smartphone. It features a simple menu and a live service that can help customers find the best and cheapest options. It also includes several financing options to help seniors save even more.
Memberships start at $15.58 for a Basic Plan (or $187/year). On top of helping connect people with rideshare services, GoGoGrandparent can connect you with delivery services for groceries, meals and prescriptions.
While it caters to families to with kids, HopSkipDrive.com provides transportation for anyone over the age of 6, and it's been expanding across the country. There are no upfront membership fees or monthly dues — you only pay for the rides you schedule. HopSkipDrive is a newer service and still expanding, so check out their website to see if your area is covered.
Another resource available to help senior citizens is NEMT (Non-Emergency Medical Transportation) programs, which provide free rides to medical appointments. Typically available through Medicaid and some Medicare Advantage plans, NEMT programs can be found in every state, including Alaska and Hawaii.
Seniors with visual impairment or mobility issues can also find free rides through ITNAmerica. The nonprofit transportation network helps seniors connect with free travel options through a variety of companies, ministries and charity organizations. You can find participating programs in your area at ridesinsight.org.
Other Ways Seniors Can Save on Transportation
For seniors still driving their own vehicle, AAA offers a variety of discounts and programs tailored to senior citizens, including discounts to 30,000 retailers. And if you haven't compared auto insurance rates lately, you could save hundreds of dollars.
Dial-a-ride programs can also be found across the country, usually managed by the same public transportation companies in your area. These programs, such as ACCESS LYNX in the Orlando area, work similarly to rideshare programs. They use shuttles to deliver customers to their chosen destinations, can schedule pick-up times and offer discounts for seniors.
When it comes to standard public transportation service, senior citizens can expect some form of discount. Buses, subways, trains and taxi services across the country usually offer senior discounts. Don't be afraid to ask about reduced fares.
If seniors are unable to drive, many local governments will offer free transportation as well. This will need official documents, such as a doctor's note and proof of income, but these programs are available in rural areas and urban centers across the country.

Uber Technologies (UBER) is one of the stocks most watched by Zacks.com visitors lately. So, it might be a good idea to review some of the factors that might affect the near-term performance of the stock.
Shares of this ride-hailing company have returned -0.2% over the past month versus the Zacks S&P 500 composite's +1.5% change. The Zacks Internet - Services industry, to which Uber belongs, has lost 0.2% over this period. Now the key question is: Where could the stock be headed in the near term?
While media releases or rumors about a substantial change in a company's business prospects usually make its stock 'trending' and lead to an immediate price change, there are always some fundamental facts that eventually dominate the buy-and-hold decision-making.
Rather than focusing on anything else, we at Zacks prioritize evaluating the change in a company's earnings projection. This is because we believe the fair value for its stock is determined by the present value of its future stream of earnings.
We essentially look at how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to reflect the impact of the latest business trends. And if earnings estimates go up for a company, the fair value for its stock goes up. A higher fair value than the current market price drives investors' interest in buying the stock, leading to its price moving higher. This is why empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements.
Uber is expected to post earnings of $0.94 per share for the current quarter, representing a year-over-year change of -69.8%. Over the last 30 days, the Zacks Consensus Estimate has changed -0.1%.
For the current fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $3.2 points to a change of -39.6% from the prior year. Over the last 30 days, this estimate has changed -0.5%.
For the next fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $4.56 indicates a change of +42.6% from what Uber is expected to report a year ago. Over the past month, the estimate has changed -0.7%.
With an impressive externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool -- the Zacks Rank -- is a more conclusive indicator of a stock's near-term price performance, as it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions. The size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, has resulted in a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) for Uber.
The chart below shows the evolution of the company's forward 12-month consensus EPS estimate:
12-month consensus EPS estimate for UBER
While earnings growth is arguably the most superior indicator of a company's financial health, nothing happens as such if a business isn't able to grow its revenues. After all, it's nearly impossible for a company to increase its earnings for an extended period without increasing its revenues. So, it's important to know a company's potential revenue growth.
For Uber, the consensus sales estimate for the current quarter of $14.74 billion indicates a year-over-year change of +9.4%. For the current and next fiscal years, $57.91 billion and $66.86 billion estimates indicate +11.3% and +15.5% changes, respectively.
Last Reported Results and Surprise History
Uber reported revenues of $14.19 billion in the last reported quarter, representing a year-over-year change of +12.2%. EPS of $1.17 for the same period compares with $0.63 a year ago.
Compared to the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $14.21 billion, the reported revenues represent a surprise of -0.13%. The EPS surprise was +40.96%.
Over the last four quarters, Uber surpassed consensus EPS estimates three times. The company topped consensus revenue estimates two times over this period.
Without considering a stock's valuation, no investment decision can be efficient. In predicting a stock's future price performance, it's crucial to determine whether its current price correctly reflects the intrinsic value of the underlying business and the company's growth prospects.
While comparing the current values of a company's valuation multiples, such as price-to-earnings (P/E), price-to-sales (P/S), and price-to-cash flow (P/CF), with its own historical values helps determine whether its stock is fairly valued, overvalued, or undervalued, comparing the company relative to its peers on these parameters gives a good sense of the reasonability of the stock's price.
The Zacks Value Style Score (part of the Zacks Style Scores system), which pays close attention to both traditional and unconventional valuation metrics to grade stocks from A to F (an A is better than a B; a B is better than a C; and so on), is pretty helpful in identifying whether a stock is overvalued, rightly valued, or temporarily undervalued.
Uber is graded D on this front, indicating that it is trading at a premium to its peers. Click here to see the values of some of the valuation metrics that have driven this grade.
The facts discussed here and much other information on Zacks.com might help determine whether or not it's worthwhile paying attention to the market buzz about Uber. However, its Zacks Rank #3 does suggest that it may perform in line with the broader market in the near term.

Booking Holdings has launched Vayo, a new AI-powered personal travel agent, and plans to invest up to $100 million as it explores a more personalized approach to trip planning and management.
Vayo is launching in private beta with a waitlist open to travelers. The planned investment depends on continued product development and market conditions. The company is designed to manage an entire trip rather than operate as a general-purpose chatbot or assistant focused on individual tasks.
Vayo can bring together existing travel reservations from a user’s inbox, organize trip details, identify missing components, and monitor prices. Because reservations are connected within a single itinerary, the platform is also designed to understand how changes to one part of a trip can affect others. For example, a flight delay could trigger warnings about a late hotel check-in or a dinner reservation that may need to be changed.
The company is part of Booking Holdings, whose portfolio includes Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda, KAYAK, and OpenTable. Vayo is being designed to work across Booking Holdings brands as well as reservations made through competing travel platforms or directly with airlines and hotels.
Vayo’s initial private beta will provide free, invite-only access focused primarily on frequent travelers. The company said the beta period will be used to gather feedback and refine the product before a broader rollout. Vayo will access only travel confirmations needed to build and manage trips rather than the rest of a user’s inbox.
Future product plans include direct booking capabilities, a native mobile application, collaborative trip planning with travel companions, and additional assistance once travelers are already on their trips.
Booking Holdings is positioning Vayo as an experiment in how AI can move beyond answering travel questions toward proactively managing the interconnected parts of a trip. The company believes personalized travel agents could anticipate user needs based on previous behavior, existing reservations, and trip context.
Vayo is led by CEO and co-founder Mike Fridgen. Booking Holdings CEO Glenn Fogel said the company is exploring how AI can reduce the amount of planning and coordination work that still falls on travelers.
KEY QUOTES:
“A trip isn’t a task, and travelers deserve more than a chatbot. With the backing of Booking Holdings, we’re building a personal travel agent that understands the entire trip, knows how you travel and never stops working for you. That’s Vayo.”
Mike Fridgen, CEO And Co-Founder Of Vayo
“Travel is one of the most complex consumer experiences, and too much of the work still falls on the traveler to manage. Booking Holdings Inc. (BKNG) Is Building Its Own AI Agent. Can Cash Flow Defend the Multiple?
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 10:11 PM CDT 5 min read
Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) is no longer only defending its travel marketplace from rival online agencies. It must also establish where its economics fit when artificial-intelligence agents can search for hotels and complete bookings for customers. On October 14, the company announced a planned $100 million investment in Vayo, a personal travel agent entering private beta. The proposed investment is small relative to Booking's approximately $120.73 billion equity valuation. Its significance therefore depends less on immediate earnings contribution and more on whether Booking remains the destination for travel transactions when discovery migrates elsewhere.
The Booking Engine Still Earns Its Place
In the second quarter of 2026, Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG)'s room nights grew 5%, gross bookings increased 9%, and adjusted EBITDA rose 9% to approximately $2.6 billion. Adjusted EPS advanced 15%, helped by a 6% lower average share count. Management also increased its expected annual transformation savings run rate to $650 million from $550 million, with most incremental savings anticipated in 2027. These are tangible offsets to the idea that an AI intermediary can simply replace Booking overnight.
The company ranks third among the 10 best undervalued stocks to buy now according to Reddit, using Q2 hedge fund ownership. But two stocks ranked ahead of it. The more relevant puzzle is whether Booking's unusually strong profitability and cash-generation record deserves a different valuation from faster-growing platforms with potentially less exposure to travel demand.
Agentic AI Threatens the Route to the Customer
The risk is not necessarily that travelers stop staying in hotels. It is that an agent captures the customer relationship, compares offers and directs transactions to whichever supplier pays the lowest effective distribution cost. Meta's Muse launch intensified that concern in September. Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) is responding with Vayo and the September 29 launch of Lola, another AI-driven booking experience backed by the company. Its defenses include deeply fragmented accommodation inventory, loyalty benefits, payment infrastructure, and a growing range of connected trip services.
Nevertheless, Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) still has a customer-acquisition bill. Second-quarter marketing expense rose 11%, faster than gross bookings, and mobile applications accounted for a high-50% share of room nights. Management said the direct-to-consumer share remained in the mid-60% range. The ability to retain direct traffic is important because a higher proportion of paid referrals could reduce the economics of each hotel night even if bookings continue to rise. Our recent comparison of Booking's profitability with Airbnb's faster-growing, differentiated supply shows why inventory, distribution and margins deserve to be considered together.
Seeking Alpha's data values Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) at 17.76 times trailing GAAP earnings and 15.31 times forward GAAP earnings; forward non-GAAP P/E is 15.37. That non-GAAP forward multiple is roughly 36% below the five-year average of 24.16, although only modestly above the sector median of 14.84. The consensus projects EPS growth of 14.59% in 2026, 18.41% in 2027, and 16.41% in 2028, a trajectory capable of reducing the prospective P/E over time if achieved.
Cash flow complicates that apparently favorable reading. The second-quarter earnings call reported $3.6 billion of free cash flow, and the company repurchased $7.4 billion of shares in the first half. But merchant bookings allow travelers' money to arrive before Booking pays accommodation providers or processes refunds. Consequently, operating cash flow can be supported by customer-related liabilities that are not distributable earnings. Our closer look at Booking's traveler advances and how much cash shareholders can actually keep addresses that important distinction.
The capital structure also deserves attention: $20.92 billion of debt sits against $17.21 billion of cash, representing approximately $3.71 billion of net debt. The balance sheet is not an immediate sign of distress, but the market's earnings multiple needs to be read alongside buybacks, working capital, and the future cost of defending customer acquisition.
Travel Weakness Makes the Timing Less Forgiving
The operating backdrop offers limited room for complacency. Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) lowered its full-year gross-bookings growth expectation in August to high single digits from high single digits to low double digits, citing pressure on international travel, particularly linked to the Middle East conflict. On October 7, Wells Fargo reduced its target to $190 from $220, Equal Weight, citing long-haul weakness and AI risks. Cantor Fitzgerald moved to $170 from $220 on October 12, Neutral, while Morgan Stanley had initiated at Overweight with a $230 target in September, emphasizing supply scale as a competitive advantage.
Hedge fund ownership slipped to 92 from 95 between Q1 and Q2 2026, while shares sold short rose to 22.62 million from 20.15 million between August 31 and September 30, or 3.02% of float. These are positioning snapshots, not proof that investors have reached a verdict on Muse. The next evidence will come from direct booking trends, marketing efficiency, room-night growth, and whether Vayo or Lola can preserve Booking's transaction economics. For a useful contrast, why Airbnb's expansion may command a higher growth multiple examines a different kind of travel-platform exposure.
While we acknowledge the risk and potential of BKNG as an investment, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. Fri, October 16, 2026 at 7:30 AM CDT 4 min read
Investors often turn to recommendations made by Wall Street analysts before making a Buy, Sell, or Hold decision about a stock. While media reports about rating changes by these brokerage-firm employed (or sell-side) analysts often affect a stock's price, do they really matter?
Let's take a look at what these Wall Street heavyweights have to say about Booking Holdings (BKNG) before we discuss the reliability of brokerage recommendations and how to use them to your advantage.
Booking Holdings currently has an average brokerage recommendation (ABR) of 1.56, on a scale of 1 to 5 (Strong Buy to Strong Sell), calculated based on the actual recommendations (Buy, Hold, Sell, etc.) made by 39 brokerage firms. An ABR of 1.56 approximates between Strong Buy and Buy.
Of the 39 recommendations that derive the current ABR, 27 are Strong Buy and two are Buy. Strong Buy and Buy respectively account for 69.2% and 5.1% of all recommendations.

The ABR suggests buying Booking Holdings, but making an investment decision solely on the basis of this information might not be a good idea. According to several studies, brokerage recommendations have little to no success guiding investors to choose stocks with the most potential for price appreciation.
Are you wondering why? The vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover often results in a strong positive bias of their analysts in rating it. Our research shows that for every "Strong Sell" recommendation, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations.
This means that the interests of these institutions are not always aligned with those of retail investors, giving little insight into the direction of a stock's future price movement. It would therefore be best to use this information to validate your own analysis or a tool that has proven to be highly effective at predicting stock price movements.
Zacks Rank, our proprietary stock rating tool with an impressive externally audited track record, categorizes stocks into five groups, ranging from Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) to Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), and is an effective indicator of a stock's price performance in the near future. Therefore, using the ABR to validate the Zacks Rank could be an efficient way of making a profitable investment decision.
Zacks Rank Should Not Be Confused With ABR
In spite of the fact that Zacks Rank and ABR both appear on a scale from 1 to 5, they are two completely different measures.
The ABR is calculated solely based on brokerage recommendations and is typically displayed with decimals (example: 1.28). In contrast, the Zacks Rank is a quantitative model allowing investors to harness the power of earnings estimate revisions. It is displayed in whole numbers -- 1 to 5.
It has been and continues to be the case that analysts employed by brokerage firms are overly optimistic with their recommendations. Because of their employers' vested interests, these analysts issue more favorable ratings than their research would support, misguiding investors far more often than helping them.
On the other hand, earnings estimate revisions are at the core of the Zacks Rank. And empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements.
Furthermore, the different grades of the Zacks Rank are applied proportionately across all stocks for which brokerage analysts provide earnings estimates for the current year. In other words, at all times, this tool maintains a balance among the five ranks it assigns.
There is also a key difference between the ABR and Zacks Rank when it comes to freshness. When you look at the ABR, it may not be up-to-date. Nonetheless, since brokerage analysts constantly revise their earnings estimates to reflect changing business trends, and their actions get reflected in the Zacks Rank quickly enough, it is always timely in predicting future stock prices.
Is BKNG Worth Investing In?
Looking at the earnings estimate revisions for Booking Holdings, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the current year has declined 0.1% over the past month to $10.48.
Analysts' growing pessimism over the company's earnings prospects, as indicated by strong agreement among them in revising EPS estimates lower, could be a legitimate reason for the stock to plunge in the near term.
The size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, has resulted in a Zacks Rank #4 (Sell) for Booking Holdings. You can see the complete list of today's Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) stocks here >>>>
Therefore, it could be wise to take the Buy-equivalent ABR for Booking Holdings with a grain of salt.

Booking Holdings Launches Vayo with Planned $100M Investment
Wed, October 14, 2026 at 7:55 AM CDT 4 min read
The waitlist opens today at vayo.com for the personal travel agent built for trips, not tasks, that organizes everything you've booked, learns how you travel and never stops working for you
SEATTLE, Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Booking Holdings (NASDAQ: BKNG) today announced a planned $100M* investment in its new company Vayo, which is launching in private beta with a waitlist now open at vayo.com. Vayo is where your trips live: a personal travel agent that knows how you travel and makes every trip better before you have to ask. Unlike a chatbot that answers questions in walls of text or an AI assistant that completes individual tasks, Vayo holds every trip together and keeps working on it long after the planning is done.
Vayo, the new personal travel agent from Booking Holdings, built for trips, not tasks.
Planning a trip often means piecing together flights, hotels, activities and reservations across multiple channels, while keeping track of confirmation numbers, plans still in progress and details yet to be booked. Vayo calls the time, effort and mental load of managing it all a "planning tax." Vayo takes on that work, bringing your existing reservations together from your inbox, filling in what's missing and watching prices. Because every booking is connected, Vayo sees how one change affects everything else: when a flight changes, Vayo flags the late check-in and the dinner reservation now at risk. It's like a thousand travel agents working for you, with the care of one who truly knows you.
"A trip isn't a task, and travelers deserve more than a chatbot," said Mike Fridgen, CEO and co-founder of Vayo. "With the backing of Booking Holdings, we're building a personal travel agent that understands the entire trip, knows how you travel and never stops working for you. That's Vayo."
As a Booking Holdings company whose portfolio includes Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda, KAYAK, and OpenTable, Vayo combines the scale and supply of the global leader in online travel with a consumer experience built from the ground up. Built on openness, Vayo works across Booking Holdings brands and beyond, including reservations made through other travel platforms or directly with airlines and hotels. Travelers rarely book an entire trip through a single source, and a personal travel agent has to work the way travelers actually do.
"Travel is one of the most complex consumer experiences, and too much of the work still falls on the traveler to manage," said Glenn Fogel, CEO of Booking Holdings. "Vayo is exploring how AI can anticipate needs to make planning and managing a trip more seamless. I have confidence in the Vayo team and their ability to move with purpose, capitalize on early learnings and adapt at pace as they explore what the next generation of personalization in travel can look like."
Vayo's private beta offers free, invite-only access initially focused on frequent travelers who feel the planning tax most: those who take multiple trips a year but don't always have the time to plan them. The beta is designed as a learning period, giving early users a direct role in shaping the product and informing what gets built next. Vayo accesses only the travel confirmations needed to build and manage trips, keeping the rest of a user's inbox private.
In the months ahead, Vayo plans to add direct booking, launch a native app and make it possible to plan trips with travel companions. It will also go deeper once a trip begins, helping travelers navigate the changes and decisions that come up along the way. The destination is a trusted travel agent in your pocket, for every trip in your life.
The waitlist is open now at vayo.com.
*Intention to invest subject to continued advancement of the product and market conditions.

What Could Lift Booking Holdings Stock?
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 6:02 AM CDT 4 min read
Shares of Booking Holdings (BKNG) have lost 17.2% over the past year, lagging the S&P 500 and its 17.4% return. Following that decline, the stock trades at 17.3 times earnings. That multiple sits below the company's average of 28.3 over its last 12 fiscal quarter ends. A lower P/E means paying less for each dollar of profit, but that discount only pays off if the profit keeps growing. So what would have to go right for Booking Holdings stock to climb from here?
Booking Holdings Would Gain Most From Selling More Travel
Selling more travel would generate most of the stock's potential gain. Under Trefis's three-year scenario, higher revenue accounts for 82.4% of the upside. That means more room nights, the nights travelers book through platforms like Booking.com, alongside more flight and attraction tickets. Following these assumptions, the stock would appreciate about 49% in three years, excluding dividends.
The table compares Booking Holdings today against the scenario three years out.
An expanding multiple provides a further 28.4% of the upside, assuming a higher P/E, while a lower margin takes 10.8% back. This scenario lifts the P/E from 17.3 to 19.4. Even after that increase, the multiple would remain below the stock's own 12-quarter average of 28.3.
Where Booking Holdings' Sales Growth Comes From
The scenario models revenue growth of 11.6% a year. That pace falls slightly behind the 12.9% Booking Holdings delivered over the twelve months to fiscal Q2 2026. Growth slowed in the latest quarter, so the scenario needs the pace to pick up again as travelers book more nights and more of the rest of their trips through the company's sites. Room nights increased 5% and revenue rose 8% in fiscal Q2 2026, management said on the August 4, 2026 call. Executives issued a slower guide for the following period, forecasting fiscal Q3 2026 revenue growth of 4% to 6%. However, that guidance covers a single quarter rather than three years, and it assumes the conflict in the Middle East keeps weighing on long-haul travel.
Booking Holdings is also capturing more business from its most loyal customers. Members of its Genius levels 2 and 3 accounted for more than 30% of active customers in fiscal Q2 2026, representing an increase from a year earlier. Management also said that trips combining several bookings grew more than twice as fast as total transactions at Booking.com.
How Booking Holdings' Upside Changes Under Other Scenarios
Each row below alters one assumption while keeping the other two from the scenario.
Revenue growth of 9.6% a year instead of 11.6%
Net margin of 21.9% in year three instead of 24.4%
P/E of 17.3 in year three instead of 19.4
5 years at the same assumptions instead of 3
The scenario already trims the net margin, because Booking Holdings currently operates at a margin above its average for the twelve quarter ends from fiscal Q2 2023 to fiscal Q1 2026. That lower margin gives back about a tenth of the gain.
Holding the stock for three years would return nothing under these assumptions if revenue shrank 2.3% a year, against the 12.9% growth Booking Holdings delivered in the twelve months to fiscal Q2 2026. The investment would also return nothing if the net margin fell to 16.4% in year three, compared to 25.5% over those twelve months. The same holds true if the P/E dropped to 13.0, against 17.3 today.
Growth in room nights is the measure to watch in the company's fiscal Q3 2026 report, expected on or around November 3, 2026.

Booking Holdings Launches Vayo With Planned $100 Million Investment In AI Personal Travel Agent
Booking Holdings has launched Vayo, a new AI-powered personal travel agent, and plans to invest up to $100 million as it explores a more personalized approach to trip planning and management.
Vayo is launching in private beta with a waitlist open to travelers. The planned investment depends on continued product development and market conditions. The company is designed to manage an entire trip rather than operate as a general-purpose chatbot or assistant focused on individual tasks.
Vayo can bring together existing travel reservations from a user’s inbox, organize trip details, identify missing components, and monitor prices. Because reservations are connected within a single itinerary, the platform is also designed to understand how changes to one part of a trip can affect others. For example, a flight delay could trigger warnings about a late hotel check-in or a dinner reservation that may need to be changed.
The company is part of Booking Holdings, whose portfolio includes Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda, KAYAK, and OpenTable. Vayo is being designed to work across Booking Holdings brands as well as reservations made through competing travel platforms or directly with airlines and hotels.
Vayo’s initial private beta will provide free, invite-only access focused primarily on frequent travelers. The company said the beta period will be used to gather feedback and refine the product before a broader rollout. Vayo will access only travel confirmations needed to build and manage trips rather than the rest of a user’s inbox.
Future product plans include direct booking capabilities, a native mobile application, collaborative trip planning with travel companions, and additional assistance once travelers are already on their trips.
Booking Holdings is positioning Vayo as an experiment in how AI can move beyond answering travel questions toward proactively managing the interconnected parts of a trip. The company believes personalized travel agents could anticipate user needs based on previous behavior, existing reservations, and trip context.
Vayo is led by CEO and co-founder Mike Fridgen. Booking Holdings CEO Glenn Fogel said the company is exploring how AI can reduce the amount of planning and coordination work that still falls on travelers.
KEY QUOTES:
“A trip isn’t a task, and travelers deserve more than a chatbot. With the backing of Booking Holdings, we’re building a personal travel agent that understands the entire trip, knows how you travel and never stops working for you. That’s Vayo.”
Mike Fridgen, CEO And Co-Founder Of Vayo
“Travel is one of the most complex consumer experiences, and too much of the work still falls on the traveler to manage. Vayo is exploring how AI can anticipate needs to make planning and managing a trip more seamless. I have confidence in the Vayo team and their ability to move with purpose, capitalize on early learnings and adapt at pace as they explore what the next generation of personalization in travel can look like.”

Booking Holdings Inc. (BKNG) Is Building Its Own AI Agent. Can Cash Flow Defend the Multiple?
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 10:11 PM CDT 5 min read
Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) is no longer only defending its travel marketplace from rival online agencies. It must also establish where its economics fit when artificial-intelligence agents can search for hotels and complete bookings for customers. On October 14, the company announced a planned $100 million investment in Vayo, a personal travel agent entering private beta. The proposed investment is small relative to Booking's approximately $120.73 billion equity valuation. Its significance therefore depends less on immediate earnings contribution and more on whether Booking remains the destination for travel transactions when discovery migrates elsewhere.
The Booking Engine Still Earns Its Place
In the second quarter of 2026, Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG)'s room nights grew 5%, gross bookings increased 9%, and adjusted EBITDA rose 9% to approximately $2.6 billion. Adjusted EPS advanced 15%, helped by a 6% lower average share count. Management also increased its expected annual transformation savings run rate to $650 million from $550 million, with most incremental savings anticipated in 2027. These are tangible offsets to the idea that an AI intermediary can simply replace Booking overnight.
The company ranks third among the 10 best undervalued stocks to buy now according to Reddit, using Q2 hedge fund ownership. But two stocks ranked ahead of it. The more relevant puzzle is whether Booking's unusually strong profitability and cash-generation record deserves a different valuation from faster-growing platforms with potentially less exposure to travel demand.
Agentic AI Threatens the Route to the Customer
The risk is not necessarily that travelers stop staying in hotels. It is that an agent captures the customer relationship, compares offers and directs transactions to whichever supplier pays the lowest effective distribution cost. Meta's Muse launch intensified that concern in September. Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) is responding with Vayo and the September 29 launch of Lola, another AI-driven booking experience backed by the company. Its defenses include deeply fragmented accommodation inventory, loyalty benefits, payment infrastructure, and a growing range of connected trip services.
Nevertheless, Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) still has a customer-acquisition bill. Second-quarter marketing expense rose 11%, faster than gross bookings, and mobile applications accounted for a high-50% share of room nights. Management said the direct-to-consumer share remained in the mid-60% range. The ability to retain direct traffic is important because a higher proportion of paid referrals could reduce the economics of each hotel night even if bookings continue to rise. Our recent comparison of Booking's profitability with Airbnb's faster-growing, differentiated supply shows why inventory, distribution and margins deserve to be considered together.
Seeking Alpha's data values Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) at 17.76 times trailing GAAP earnings and 15.31 times forward GAAP earnings; forward non-GAAP P/E is 15.37. That non-GAAP forward multiple is roughly 36% below the five-year average of 24.16, although only modestly above the sector median of 14.84. The consensus projects EPS growth of 14.59% in 2026, 18.41% in 2027, and 16.41% in 2028, a trajectory capable of reducing the prospective P/E over time if achieved.
Cash flow complicates that apparently favorable reading. The second-quarter earnings call reported $3.6 billion of free cash flow, and the company repurchased $7.4 billion of shares in the first half. But merchant bookings allow travelers' money to arrive before Booking pays accommodation providers or processes refunds. Consequently, operating cash flow can be supported by customer-related liabilities that are not distributable earnings. Our closer look at Booking's traveler advances and how much cash shareholders can actually keep addresses that important distinction.
The capital structure also deserves attention: $20.92 billion of debt sits against $17.21 billion of cash, representing approximately $3.71 billion of net debt. The balance sheet is not an immediate sign of distress, but the market's earnings multiple needs to be read alongside buybacks, working capital, and the future cost of defending customer acquisition.
Travel Weakness Makes the Timing Less Forgiving
The operating backdrop offers limited room for complacency. Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) lowered its full-year gross-bookings growth expectation in August to high single digits from high single digits to low double digits, citing pressure on international travel, particularly linked to the Middle East conflict. On October 7, Wells Fargo reduced its target to $190 from $220, Equal Weight, citing long-haul weakness and AI risks. Cantor Fitzgerald moved to $170 from $220 on October 12, Neutral, while Morgan Stanley had initiated at Overweight with a $230 target in September, emphasizing supply scale as a competitive advantage.
Hedge fund ownership slipped to 92 from 95 between Q1 and Q2 2026, while shares sold short rose to 22.62 million from 20.15 million between August 31 and September 30, or 3.02% of float. These are positioning snapshots, not proof that investors have reached a verdict on Muse. The next evidence will come from direct booking trends, marketing efficiency, room-night growth, and whether Vayo or Lola can preserve Booking's transaction economics. For a useful contrast, why Airbnb's expansion may command a higher growth multiple examines a different kind of travel-platform exposure.
While we acknowledge the risk and potential of BKNG as an investment, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. If you are looking for an AI stock that is more promising than BKNG and that has 10,000% upside potential, check out our report about this cheapest AI stock.

Booking Holdings CEO and President, Glenn Fogel On AI, Humans, and the Future of Travel
At the TIME100 AI event, leaders from across industries gathered to explore how artificial intelligence is reshaping the way we work and navigate an increasingly technology-driven world. Among them was Glenn Fogel, Chief Executive Officer and President of Booking Holdings, who offered a perspective grounded in one of the most universal human experiences: travel.
For Fogel, AI’s potential is not simply about making it easier to book a flight or hotel. It is about fundamentally changing the experience of planning a trip, and making travel more predictable and responsive. While people love to travel, he noted, the process of getting there can still be frustratingly complex. The challenge is often less about the trip itself than the uncertainty surrounding it: What happens when plans change?
AI, he suggested, could help address those pain points by anticipating what travelers need before they ask. Rather than simply responding to a search, an AI-powered travel experience could predict disruptions and adapt an itinerary in real time. If rain is forecast during a planned canal ride in Amsterdam, for example, AI could suggest moving the activity to a better day and finding another experience in its place.
That vision reflects a broader shift in how AI could interact with consumers: not simply responding to requests, but anticipating needs before they arise.
But Fogel also acknowledged that technological progress comes with responsibilities. The pace of AI-driven change, he said, raises important questions about how societies and economies will adapt. While AI promises meaningful advances, its broader effects—including potential disruption to jobs and communities—must remain part of the conversation.
At TIME100 AI, Fogel explored both sides of that equation: the opportunity to make travel more seamless and intuitive, and the responsibility to navigate an accelerating technological transition thoughtfully.

Wall Street Analysts Think Booking Holdings (BKNG) Is a Good Investment: Is It?
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 7:30 AM CDT 4 min read
Investors often turn to recommendations made by Wall Street analysts before making a Buy, Sell, or Hold decision about a stock. While media reports about rating changes by these brokerage-firm employed (or sell-side) analysts often affect a stock's price, do they really matter?
Let's take a look at what these Wall Street heavyweights have to say about Booking Holdings (BKNG) before we discuss the reliability of brokerage recommendations and how to use them to your advantage.
Booking Holdings currently has an average brokerage recommendation (ABR) of 1.56, on a scale of 1 to 5 (Strong Buy to Strong Sell), calculated based on the actual recommendations (Buy, Hold, Sell, etc.) made by 39 brokerage firms. An ABR of 1.56 approximates between Strong Buy and Buy.
Of the 39 recommendations that derive the current ABR, 27 are Strong Buy and two are Buy. Strong Buy and Buy respectively account for 69.2% and 5.1% of all recommendations.
Brokerage Recommendation Trends for BKNG
Check price target & stock forecast for Booking Holdings here>>>
The ABR suggests buying Booking Holdings, but making an investment decision solely on the basis of this information might not be a good idea. According to several studies, brokerage recommendations have little to no success guiding investors to choose stocks with the most potential for price appreciation.
Are you wondering why? The vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover often results in a strong positive bias of their analysts in rating it. Our research shows that for every "Strong Sell" recommendation, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations.
This means that the interests of these institutions are not always aligned with those of retail investors, giving little insight into the direction of a stock's future price movement. It would therefore be best to use this information to validate your own analysis or a tool that has proven to be highly effective at predicting stock price movements.
Zacks Rank, our proprietary stock rating tool with an impressive externally audited track record, categorizes stocks into five groups, ranging from Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) to Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), and is an effective indicator of a stock's price performance in the near future. Therefore, using the ABR to validate the Zacks Rank could be an efficient way of making a profitable investment decision.
Zacks Rank Should Not Be Confused With ABR
In spite of the fact that Zacks Rank and ABR both appear on a scale from 1 to 5, they are two completely different measures.
The ABR is calculated solely based on brokerage recommendations and is typically displayed with decimals (example: 1.28). In contrast, the Zacks Rank is a quantitative model allowing investors to harness the power of earnings estimate revisions. It is displayed in whole numbers -- 1 to 5.
It has been and continues to be the case that analysts employed by brokerage firms are overly optimistic with their recommendations. Because of their employers' vested interests, these analysts issue more favorable ratings than their research would support, misguiding investors far more often than helping them.
On the other hand, earnings estimate revisions are at the core of the Zacks Rank. And empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements.
Furthermore, the different grades of the Zacks Rank are applied proportionately across all stocks for which brokerage analysts provide earnings estimates for the current year. In other words, at all times, this tool maintains a balance among the five ranks it assigns.
There is also a key difference between the ABR and Zacks Rank when it comes to freshness. When you look at the ABR, it may not be up-to-date. Nonetheless, since brokerage analysts constantly revise their earnings estimates to reflect changing business trends, and their actions get reflected in the Zacks Rank quickly enough, it is always timely in predicting future stock prices.
Is BKNG Worth Investing In?
Looking at the earnings estimate revisions for Booking Holdings, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the current year has declined 0.1% over the past month to $10.48.
Analysts' growing pessimism over the company's earnings prospects, as indicated by strong agreement among them in revising EPS estimates lower, could be a legitimate reason for the stock to plunge in the near term.
The size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, has resulted in a Zacks Rank #4 (Sell) for Booking Holdings. You can see the complete list of today's Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) stocks here >>>>

The waitlist opens today at vayo.com for the personal travel agent built for trips, not tasks, that organizes everything you've booked, learns how you travel and never stops working for you
SEATTLE, Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Booking Holdings (NASDAQ: BKNG) today announced a planned $100M* investment in its new company Vayo, which is launching in private beta with a waitlist now open at vayo.com. Vayo is where your trips live: a personal travel agent that knows how you travel and makes every trip better before you have to ask. Unlike a chatbot that answers questions in walls of text or an AI assistant that completes individual tasks, Vayo holds every trip together and keeps working on it long after the planning is done.
Vayo, the new personal travel agent from Booking Holdings, built for trips, not tasks.
Planning a trip often means piecing together flights, hotels, activities and reservations across multiple channels, while keeping track of confirmation numbers, plans still in progress and details yet to be booked. Vayo calls the time, effort and mental load of managing it all a "planning tax." Vayo takes on that work, bringing your existing reservations together from your inbox, filling in what's missing and watching prices. Because every booking is connected, Vayo sees how one change affects everything else: when a flight changes, Vayo flags the late check-in and the dinner reservation now at risk. It's like a thousand travel agents working for you, with the care of one who truly knows you.
"A trip isn't a task, and travelers deserve more than a chatbot," said Mike Fridgen, CEO and co-founder of Vayo. "With the backing of Booking Holdings, we're building a personal travel agent that understands the entire trip, knows how you travel and never stops working for you. That's Vayo."
As a Booking Holdings company whose portfolio includes Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda, KAYAK, and OpenTable, Vayo combines the scale and supply of the global leader in online travel with a consumer experience built from the ground up. Built on openness, Vayo works across Booking Holdings brands and beyond, including reservations made through other travel platforms or directly with airlines and hotels. Travelers rarely book an entire trip through a single source, and a personal travel agent has to work the way travelers actually do.
"Travel is one of the most complex consumer experiences, and too much of the work still falls on the traveler to manage," said Glenn Fogel, CEO of Booking Holdings. "Vayo is exploring how AI can anticipate needs to make planning and managing a trip more seamless. I have confidence in the Vayo team and their ability to move with purpose, capitalize on early learnings and adapt at pace as they explore what the next generation of personalization in travel can look like."
Vayo's private beta offers free, invite-only access initially focused on frequent travelers who feel the planning tax most: those who take multiple trips a year but don't always have the time to plan them. The beta is designed as a learning period, giving early users a direct role in shaping the product and informing what gets built next. Vayo accesses only the travel confirmations needed to build and manage trips, keeping the rest of a user's inbox private.
In the months ahead, Vayo plans to add direct booking, launch a native app and make it possible to plan trips with travel companions. It will also go deeper once a trip begins, helping travelers navigate the changes and decisions that come up along the way. The destination is a trusted travel agent in your pocket, for every trip in your life.
The waitlist is open now at vayo.com.
*Intention to invest subject to continued advancement of the product and market conditions.

It knows how you travel with unprecedented depth, brings every detail together, and keeps working after booking to make each trip better. It's like a thousand travel agents working for you, with the care of one who truly knows you. Vayo works across the travel industry, and its only agenda is your agenda. Our mission is to make it easier for everyone to experience the world. For more information, visit BookingHoldings.com and follow us on X @BookingHoldings.

A fast-paced travel agent making bookings for a family vacation package.
Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) generated $6.934 billion of first-half operating cash flow. The June-quarter filing recorded a $4.207 billion positive cash movement from deferred merchant bookings and other current liabilities. That combined line represented 61% of operating cash flow, making its timing material to the shareholder story.
Deferred merchant bookings reached $10.1 billion at June 30. These advances include amounts payable to travel providers and Booking's own expected revenue. Most are subject to refunds for cancellations. The balance therefore cannot be treated as a reserve entirely available for repurchases.
The merchant model can improve convenience for travelers and partners while bringing payments onto Booking's platform. It also increases transaction costs. Second-quarter merchant revenue rose 15%, while agency revenue declined 7%, illustrating the changing mix. Growth in merchant collections supports the business case, but future supplier settlements and refunds accompany that growth.
Our Check Point analysis shows why the source of a company's liquidity changes the capital-return conclusion. Booking's obligation is tied to travel transactions; evaluating it requires following collections through the completed stay and provider payment.
Q2 2026 brought 92 Booking holders in Insider Monkey's database, down from 95 in Q1. Orbis increased its common-share position 290% to 7.192 million shares, despite the lower overall holder count.
The first-half payout exceeded cash after investment
Subtracting $183 million of equipment spending leaves $6.751 billion of first-half free cash flow on a simple operating-cash-less-capex basis. Booking paid $7.758 billion for repurchases and $664 million in dividends, exceeding that amount by $1.671 billion. New debt proceeds and existing liquidity provided additional funding. The gap shows that repeating the payout pace requires more cash, reduced distributions or another funding source.
Removing the entire $4.207 billion liability movement would be equally misleading. That line includes other liabilities, and the rest of working capital also moved. It cannot by itself supply a normalized cash estimate.
At October 9 prices, Booking traded at 12.6 times reported trailing free cash flow, equivalent to a 7.9% yield. The full-year window is more useful than annualizing a seasonally strong first half, though changes in advance collections still affect it. Growing travel demand and payment adoption can support earnings; slower bookings or higher cancellations can reduce funding before a trailing multiple reflects the change.
Shareholders should watch subsequent cash statements for whether completed travel and supplier settlements sustain cash after investment, alongside a repurchase pace that fits those receipts.

What Could Lift Booking Holdings Stock?
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 6:02 AM CDT 4 min read
Shares of Booking Holdings (BKNG) have lost 17.2% over the past year, lagging the S&P 500 and its 17.4% return. Following that decline, the stock trades at 17.3 times earnings. That multiple sits below the company's average of 28.3 over its last 12 fiscal quarter ends. A lower P/E means paying less for each dollar of profit, but that discount only pays off if the profit keeps growing. So what would have to go right for Booking Holdings stock to climb from here?
Booking Holdings Would Gain Most From Selling More Travel
Selling more travel would generate most of the stock's potential gain. Under Trefis's three-year scenario, higher revenue accounts for 82.4% of the upside. That means more room nights, the nights travelers book through platforms like Booking.com, alongside more flight and attraction tickets. Following these assumptions, the stock would appreciate about 49% in three years, excluding dividends.
The table compares Booking Holdings today against the scenario three years out.
An expanding multiple provides a further 28.4% of the upside, assuming a higher P/E, while a lower margin takes 10.8% back. This scenario lifts the P/E from 17.3 to 19.4. Even after that increase, the multiple would remain below the stock's own 12-quarter average of 28.3.
Where Booking Holdings' Sales Growth Comes From
The scenario models revenue growth of 11.6% a year. That pace falls slightly behind the 12.9% Booking Holdings delivered over the twelve months to fiscal Q2 2026. Growth slowed in the latest quarter, so the scenario needs the pace to pick up again as travelers book more nights and more of the rest of their trips through the company's sites. Room nights increased 5% and revenue rose 8% in fiscal Q2 2026, management said on the August 4, 2026 call. Executives issued a slower guide for the following period, forecasting fiscal Q3 2026 revenue growth of 4% to 6%. However, that guidance covers a single quarter rather than three years, and it assumes the conflict in the Middle East keeps weighing on long-haul travel.
Booking Holdings is also capturing more business from its most loyal customers. Members of its Genius levels 2 and 3 accounted for more than 30% of active customers in fiscal Q2 2026, representing an increase from a year earlier. Management also said that trips combining several bookings grew more than twice as fast as total transactions at Booking.com.
How Booking Holdings' Upside Changes Under Other Scenarios
Each row below alters one assumption while keeping the other two from the scenario.
Revenue growth of 9.6% a year instead of 11.6%
Net margin of 21.9% in year three instead of 24.4%
P/E of 17.3 in year three instead of 19.4
5 years at the same assumptions instead of 3
The scenario already trims the net margin, because Booking Holdings currently operates at a margin above its average for the twelve quarter ends from fiscal Q2 2023 to fiscal Q1 2026. That lower margin gives back about a tenth of the gain.
Holding the stock for three years would return nothing under these assumptions if revenue shrank 2.3% a year, against the 12.9% growth Booking Holdings delivered in the twelve months to fiscal Q2 2026. The investment would also return nothing if the net margin fell to 16.4% in year three, compared to 25.5% over those twelve months. The same holds true if the P/E dropped to 13.0, against 17.3 today.
Growth in room nights is the measure to watch in the company's fiscal Q3 2026 report, expected on or around November 3, 2026.
How To Act On BKNG?
Not necessarily on Booking Holdings alone, if your goal is long-term wealth. Wealth is built by owning the companies that keep outperforming, the leaders of their industries, wherever they are. Here are two companies from Booking Holdings' own industry that have beaten it. Over the five years to October 2026, Royal Caribbean stock rose 245% and Lindblad Expeditions stock rose 131%, while Booking Holdings stock rose 69%.
Finding companies like these takes comparison across industries and sectors, and that is what the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio does. It holds 30 quality companies in equal weight and, since its inception in September 2020, has returned more than 105%, ahead of a benchmark that combines the S&P 500, S&P Mid-cap and Russell 2000. Vayo, Booking Holdings' second AI-native startup, launched Wednesday in private beta with a waitlist at vayo.com. It is built to become the place where travelers manage their entire trip, including reservations made outside Booking's own brands.
Booking Holdings plans to invest $100 million in the startup, subject to continued advancement of the product and market conditions. Booking had previously disclosed that it was giving both Vayo and Lola, its other internally funded AI startup unveiled about two weeks earlier, a greenfield mandate to build new businesses beyond its established brands.

Company: BKNG
Jan research (many sources; citations and numbers checked by code against each source):
- Booking Holdings launched Vayo, an AI-powered personal travel agent, with plans to invest up to $100 million in its development. [https://pulse2.com/booking-holdings-launches-vayo-with-planned-100-million-investment-in-ai-personal-travel-agent/] (2026-10-20; NEW)
- Vayo is in private beta with a waitlist open to travelers and aims to manage entire trips by integrating reservations from multiple sources. [https://pulse2.com/booking-holdings-launches-vayo-with-planned-100-million-investment-in-ai-personal-travel-agent/] (2026-10-20; NEW)
- Vayo is designed to work across Booking Holdings brands and external travel reservations, monitoring trip changes and their impacts. [https://pulse2.com/booking-holdings-launches-vayo-with-planned-100-million-investment-in-ai-personal-travel-agent/] (2026-10-20; NEW)
- Booking Holdings launched Vayo, an AI-powered personal travel agent, with plans for up to $100 million investment in its development. [https://pulse2.com/booking-holdings-launches-vayo-with-planned-100-million-investment-in-ai-personal-travel-agent/] (2026-10-20; NEW)
- Vayo is launching in private beta with invite-only access for frequent travelers to gather feedback before broader rollout. [https://pulse2.com/booking-holdings-launches-vayo-with-planned-100-million-investment-in-ai-personal-travel-agent/] (2026-10-20; NEW)
- Vayo manages entire trips by integrating travel reservations from user's inbox, organizing details, identifying missing components, and monitoring price changes. [https://pulse2.com/booking-holdings-launches-vayo-with-planned-100-million-investment-in-ai-personal-travel-agent/] (2026-10-20; NEW)
- Vayo will access only travel confirmations needed to build and manage trips, not the entire user inbox. [https://pulse2.com/booking-holdings-launches-vayo-with-planned-100-million-investment-in-ai-personal-travel-agent/] (2026-10-20; NEW)
- Future Vayo features include direct booking capabilities, mobile app, collaborative trip planning, and in-trip assistance. [https://pulse2.com/booking-holdings-launches-vayo-with-planned-100-million-investment-in-ai-personal-travel-agent/] (2026-10-20; NEW)
- Vayo is designed to work across Booking Holdings brands and competing travel platforms. [https://pulse2.com/booking-holdings-launches-vayo-with-planned-100-million-investment-in-ai-personal-travel-agent/] (2026-10-20; NEW)
- Booking Holdings CEO Glenn Fogel stated Vayo aims to reduce planning and coordination work on travelers through AI. [https://pulse2.com/booking-holdings-launches-vayo-with-planned-100-million-investment-in-ai-personal-travel-agent/] (2026-10-20; NEW)
- Booking Holdings (BKNG) shares returned -6.3% over the past month vs Zacks S&P 500 composite's +2.1% change [https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/booking-holdings-inc-bkng-attracting-120005712.html] (2026-10-15; NEW)
- BKNG's current quarter earnings estimate is $4.48 EPS, up +12.6% YoY [https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/booking-holdings-inc-bkng-attracting-120005712.html] (2026-10-15; NEW)

text: Booking Holdings Launches Vayo With Planned $100 Million Investment In AI Personal Travel Agent Booking Holdings has launched Vayo, a new AI-powered personal travel agent, and plans to invest up to $100 million as it explores a more personalized approach to trip planning and management. Vayo is launching in private beta with a waitlist open to travelers. The planned investment depends on continued product development and market conditions. The company is designed to manage an entire trip rather than operate as a general-purpose chatbot or assistant focused on individual tasks. Vayo can bring together existing travel reservations from a user’s inbox, organize trip details, identify missing components, and monitor prices. Because reservations are connected within a single itinerary, the platform is also designed to understand how changes to one part of a trip can affect others. For example, a flight delay could trigger warnings about a late hotel check-in or a dinner reservation that may need to be changed. The company is part of Booking Holdings, whose portfolio includes Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda, KAYAK, and OpenTable. Vayo is being designed to work across Booking Holdings brands as well as reservations made through competing travel platforms or directly with airlines and hotels. Vayo’s initial private beta will provide free, invite-only access focused primarily on frequent travelers. The company said the beta period will be used to gather feedback and refine the product before a broader rollout. Vayo will access only travel confirmations needed to build and manage trips rather than the rest of a user’s inbox. Future product plans include direct booking capabilities, a native mobile application, collaborative trip planning with travel companions, and additional assistance once travelers are already on their trips. Booking Holdings is positioning Vayo as an experiment in how AI can move beyond answering travel questions toward proactively managing the interconnected parts of a trip. The company believes personalized travel agents could anticipate user needs based on previous behavior, existing reservations, and trip context. Vayo is led by CEO and co-founder Mike Fridgen. Booking Holdings CEO Glenn Fogel said the company is exploring how AI can reduce the amount of planning and coordination work that still falls on travelers. Teradyne, Inc. announced a production-ready system that delivers enhanced burn-in capabilities on its Titan HP platform. Traditional burn-in holds devices in banks of dedicated ovens at a controlled air temperature for hours before they move on to functional test. Teradyne Titan HP instead holds each device at its target junction temperature while running a realistic device workload, so reliability stress functions are optimized and thermal controls are enabled at the per-device level. Titan HP can be used for system level test or reliability testing, optimizing capital cost investments. For reliability testing, every device carries its full stress-and-test history on a single record.
Teradyne introduces Titan HP with burn-in for advanced AI data center devices
Per-site thermal control, tuned to each device’s thermal and force zones, a.nd paired with high per-device kilowatt power delivery, lets Titan HP sustain reliability-stress conditions on parts whose power draw and heat dissipation strain a conventional oven flow. The platform’s asynchronous slot architecture loads and tests each slot independently, so a long stress run on one device does not idle the rest of the system, and individual sites can be serviced while the system continues to operate.
Test programs run on the Teradyne Atlas software platform, which lets engineers import existing programs or build new ones and port them to other Teradyne system level test systems. Teradyne’s per-device power roadmap extends to the levels future AI accelerators are expected to require, so the same platform carries customers forward as device power grows.
Burn-in has long been standard for automotive and other high-reliability silicon. AI accelerators and cloud infrastructure devices are now entering the same category, driven by the high cost of a single failed accelerator in a deployed rack. U.S.-based Teradyne announced that it has enhanced reliability testing for AI semiconductor equipment.
The company aims to achieve both quality and production efficiency through per-chip temperature control and test history tracking.
A hint for work: in addition to asking "is it finished?", ask "have I verified it under the conditions in which it will be used?"
In discussions about AI, attention often turns to the semiconductors that perform calculations or the convenient services they power. Behind the scenes, U.S.-based Teradyne is a company that handles the equipment used to verify whether these semiconductors function as expected.
On October 6, 2026 (local time), the company announced that it has enhanced the burn-in functionality of its semiconductor test equipment, the "Titan HP." Burn-in is a test that verifies component reliability by applying loads such as temperature and power. [1]
The equipment itself was already announced in October 2025. [3] The news this time lies in the fact that the reliability testing capabilities of the existing equipment have been strengthened. The company explains that the enhanced version has begun shipping and is already being used on production floors. [1]
Regarding conventional methods, the company explains that the process involves managing the ambient air temperature in a dedicated oven for a certain period before proceeding to verify functionality.
With the Titan HP, the internal temperature of each chip is maintained at a target value while running processes close to actual usage. The concept is to verify the chip by combining operation and temperature to approximate the conditions during real-world use.
According to the product page, the entire system can continue to operate even while individual test sites are being serviced. The load and test history for each component are also consolidated into a single record. This is a mechanism that allows for tracking what was verified and under what conditions. [2]
What can be expected and what remains unknown
The company states that this can reduce inspection costs and floor space, as well as shorten the time to market for products. This is the expectation presented by the company. This announcement does not include specific comparative results, such as by what percentage costs were reduced or how much the failure rate improved. [1]
Furthermore, one cannot judge that the same effect will be achieved for all customers based solely on the explanation that it is "being used on production floors." The actual effect must be viewed in the context of the items being inspected and the operational conditions.
In corporate news, it is easier to understand if one separates the fact that a product has been released from the results expected thereafter. It is also important not to interpret the announcement of a new feature directly as an increase in sales or profits.
What can be gleaned from this announcement is that making quality verification easier to incorporate into daily tasks is also a form of product value. This is an interpretation based on the content of the announcement.
For example, a business tool that works with a small amount of data might produce different results during concentrated end-of-month processing. Even if a procedure manual is easy for the creator to understand, it may be difficult for someone handling it for the first time. The significance of adding the perspective of "how it is actually used" to the verification of completion applies to more than just semiconductors.

Under the award program, nominations are submitted by TÜV Rheinland North America by sales or field leadership and evaluated by a panel of three to five experts using predefined weighted criteria to ensure transparency and integrity in the selection process. Teradyne is the second annual winner of this award following the inaugural winner P&G.

AI Chips Need Testing, and Teradyne (TER) Is Winning. Is the Valuation Too High?
Robots get the headlines at Teradyne (NASDAQ:TER). Chip testers pay the bills. In the second quarter of 2026, the company's robotics arm brought in $100 million. Its semiconductor test business brought in $1.12 billion over the same three months.
That split matters, because the stock isn't cheap. Teradyne builds the machines that check chips for defects before they ship, a step every AI processor and memory chip has to clear. It also owns Universal Robots, a maker of collaborative robot arms (cobots, built to work beside people) found on factory floors around the world. That operational momentum earns the stock a spot among the 10 High-Beta Stocks with Strong Revenue Growth. So what are investors actually paying for at 44 times expected earnings? The answer depends less on the robots than on how long the testing boom lasts.
AI Chips Need Testing, and Teradyne (TER) Is Winning. Is the Valuation Too High?
The second quarter was Teradyne's second straight record. Revenue hit $1.33 billion, up 104% from $652 million a year earlier, and beat the top of management's own guidance. Adjusted (non-GAAP) earnings per share came in at $2.47, against $0.57 a year before.
Memory was a big driver. Teradyne posted record memory revenue on continued DRAM strength and a revival in NAND final test, the last check flash chips get before shipping. The AI build-out is clearly pulling on more than just processors; a tailwind memory chipmakers like Micron are riding too.
Pricing power shows up in the margins. Gross margin came in at 59.8%, and CEO Greg Smith said rising wafer fab equipment spending sets the company up for growth in 2027 and beyond.
Robotics is small, but it's no longer just about arms. At the Automate trade show earlier this year, Teradyne Robotics showed off what it calls production-ready physical AI, robots that adapt to messy surroundings instead of repeating one motion. Its first physical AI product, the MiR1200 Pallet Jack, is already for sale.
The more telling detail was who else showed up. Partners demonstrated AI bin picking from Vention, imitation-learning tools built with Scale AI, and dual-arm robots threading copper cables into server racks, all running on Universal Robots hardware. Teradyne also taps Nvidia's GR00T model and Isaac Sim simulation software. When outside developers build on your arms, the platform starts to look like a standard, which keeps Teradyne in the conversation about robotics stocks betting on physical AI.
Has the Testing Cycle Peaked?
Here's the worry. Teradyne guided third-quarter revenue to $1.2 billion to $1.3 billion, below the record $1.33 billion it posted in the second quarter. Adjusted EPS guidance of $1.85 to $2.15 also sits under the second quarter's $2.47. Gross margin had already slipped to 59.8% from 60.9% in the first quarter.
Chip testing has always been cyclical, and a step down after a record can be the first sign of a plateau. Robotics, at $100 million a quarter, is far too small to cushion a semiconductor slowdown. Management's guidance still credits strong AI-related demand, though, and its 2027 outlook doesn't read like a company bracing for a bust. One softer quarter wouldn't break the story. Two in a row would, leaving valuation-conscious investors looking elsewhere, as Teradyne misses out on the 10 Best Affordable Stocks to Buy According to Wall Street Analysts.
At 44.29 times forward earnings, as of October 12, Teradyne trades well above the sector's 23.29. It also sits above its own five-year average of 35.27, so investors are paying up even by Teradyne's standards.
Growth is the defense. Analysts expect earnings to grow 28.17% in 2027. That's fast, but it doesn't fully explain a multiple this far above the stock's own history. The price assumes AI testing demand keeps rolling for years and that robotics eventually becomes a real earnings contributor rather than a side story. It's the same tension running through AI chip equipment stocks, where booming orders meet stretched multiples.
Short interest sits at 6.38% of the float, meaning a noticeable slice of traders is betting the rally has gone too far. Hedge funds moved the other way, with 82 holding the stock in the most recent quarter, up from 80 in the prior one.
The evidence says investors are paying for the testing boom, with robotics as an option on top. That boom is real, and the 2027 growth forecast gives the premium some cover. The setup suits growth investors who can stomach chip-cycle swings and believe AI test demand lasts into 2027. If the third quarter lands inside guidance and management holds its 2027 view, 44 times earnings looks defensible. A second straight sequential decline, or fading memory strength, would make it look like peak pricing.
While we acknowledge the risk and potential of TER as an investment, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. The production-ready system runs device workloads at target junction temperatures and records each device’s stress history.
Teradyne, Inc. announced a production-ready system that delivers enhanced burn-in capabilities on its Titan HP platform. Traditional burn-in holds devices in banks of dedicated ovens at a controlled air temperature for hours before they move on to functional test. Teradyne Titan HP instead holds each device at its target junction temperature while running a realistic device workload, so reliability stress functions are optimized and thermal controls are enabled at the per-device level. Titan HP can be used for system level test or reliability testing, optimizing capital cost investments. For reliability testing, every device carries its full stress-and-test history on a single record.
Teradyne introduces Titan HP with burn-in for advanced AI data center devices
Per-site thermal control, tuned to each device’s thermal and force zones, a.nd paired with high per-device kilowatt power delivery, lets Titan HP sustain reliability-stress conditions on parts whose power draw and heat dissipation strain a conventional oven flow. The platform’s asynchronous slot architecture loads and tests each slot independently, so a long stress run on one device does not idle the rest of the system, and individual sites can be serviced while the system continues to operate.
Test programs run on the Teradyne Atlas software platform, which lets engineers import existing programs or build new ones and port them to other Teradyne system level test systems. Teradyne’s per-device power roadmap extends to the levels future AI accelerators are expected to require, so the same platform carries customers forward as device power grows.
Burn-in has long been standard for automotive and other high-reliability silicon. AI accelerators and cloud infrastructure devices are now entering the same category, driven by the high cost of a single failed accelerator in a deployed rack. That demand is arriving as capital, floor space, and handling capacity for dedicated oven banks come under pressure in high-volume manufacturing and OSAT facilities.
Enhanced burn-in extends Teradyne’s test portfolio, which spans the AI device supply chain from wafer to data center. As AI silicon moves through wafer probe, package test, system level test, and now reliability stress testing, Teradyne covers every device at every insertion.
Teradyne Titan HP with enhanced burn-in is available now and deployed in production.
For more information, visit teradyne.com/titan-hp.
